abstract.div:
Time-triggered Systems-of-Systems (SoS)
promise to satisfy the real-time and dependability requirements of safetyrelevant applications such as medical systems, smart manufacturing and defense systems. However, the time-triggered scheduling algorithms in the state-of-the-art were developed for monolithic systems and they do not support the requirements and constraints of SoS. Scheduling tasks and optimizing the resource allocation in SoS is more complex than in monolithic systems due to the autonomy of its constituting systems, the lack of central control, and no global information about the resources in different constituent systems.
In this article, we propose a two-level interactive heuristic approach using a Genetic Algorithm (GA) to schedule realtime applications incrementally by adding them to the timetriggered SoS. We compute and deploy the schedule for each new SoS application at runtime after its arrival. Therefore, the limited communication and computational resources must be shared between different SoS applications released over time. By reducing the blocking time of shared resources, we can cope with the possible shortage of resources for future applications. Therefore, we develop a new resource allocation algorithm which creates more balance in the blocking times of shared resources and helps to satisfy future resource requests. We generate example scenarios to examine the schedulability of our new incremental scheduling algorithm. The experimental results show that the proposed optimization scheme compared to an incremental scheduler without blocking time considerations can find a better schedule for a sequence of applications.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: In recent years, the functionality of distributed systems with strict timing requirements has increased significantly. Therefore, there is a trend towards applying time-triggered systems due to their predictability and dependability [1]. These strengths simplify testing and certification, however, timetriggered scheduling is still a challenging task especially for complex systems.

A System of Systems (SoS) emerges from the collaboration of multiple independent systems in order to accomplish a higher level purpose. These systems are normally provided by different organizations and with different implementation technologies. There are unique characteristics that distinguish an SoS from classic complex systems including geographical distribution, operational and managerial independence of its constituent systems, emergent behavior and evolutionary development processes [2]. Facing today's interconnected world, SoS can be applied in a broad range of environments [3]. First, they were deployed in the defense sector but now they provide services in different sectors and industries including transportation, energy, health care, media, and financial businesses [4]. As a real-world example of an SoS application, we consider a medical monitoring system. In this system, there are different organizations and parties involved such as a hospital, a medical doctor, a medical data center and a patient. The medical monitoring system is an SoS, which should provide a reliable service, i.e., detecting a medical emergency when the patient is alone at home, with temporal guarantees. The doctor can be considered as an initiator and establishes the medical monitoring system at the patient home after leaving the hospital. When the admission is completed and the SoS application was scheduled, the medical monitoring application starts to work with reliability and realtime requirements.

SoS networks may encounter different applications which are introduced and/or removed over time, while sharing the underlying resources of the constituent systems. The lack of an appropriate customized scheduling strategy will cause the shortage of resources which could result in catastrophic outcomes in safety-critical domains such as health care systems. The main optimization challenge that we face in a time-triggered SoS is the temporal and spatial coordination of the autonomous constituent systems including the service allocation and the shared resource access, while satisfying the temporal constraints of real-time applications. Moreover, there are possible conflicting goals between the SoS and its constituent systems besides the lack of central control and global knowledge w.r.t. internals of constituent systems.

In scheduling an SoS application, each constituent system is only aware of its own resources and takes care of scheduling its operations independently, which means there is no need to share information with any central authority about how to utilize resources. However, in case of releasing a sequence of applications, local schedulers should update their resource allocation approach accordingly. Therefore, the resource allocation mechanism should contemplate not only the timing constraints of the current SoS application but also the schedulability of applications introduced in the future.

In this paper, we propose two GA-based schedulers for scheduling SoS applications incrementally by adding them to the time-triggered SoS. The first incremental scheduler assigns resources based on a conventional allocation approach, i.e., assigning the earliest feasible time slot to operations, in order to schedule the application in the shortest period of time. Applying this approach results in a good solution for the first application but with emerging new applications, the chance of finding feasible solutions is low. Therefore, we propose a new scheduler based on an evaluation measure named Maximum Blocking Time (MBT) to improve the allocation by considering more dispersed busy time slots for resources and preventing long blocking times. The fitness function in the new scheduler resembles the trade-off between the MBT of resources and the makespan of each application. As a result, the new approach may generate non ideal solutions for individual applications from the makespan point of view, but there is a better chance of finding feasible schedules for later applications. We generate a scenario of multiple real-time SoS applications arriving dynamically over time in a time-triggered SoS and compare the schedulability of these two incremental schedulers.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows: Section II reviews the related work. Section III describes the SoS architecture from the logical and physical points of view. Section IV explains the proposed incremental scheduling algorithm and two different mechanism of resource allocation. Section V analyzes the merit of the new incremental scheduler and evaluates its schedulability. Finally, the last section presents concluding remarks.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: Because of the unique attributes of an SoS, conventional system design assumptions and tools cannot be applied. Therefore, there are still open research challenges in architectural design, management and optimization of such systems. There are several notable studies in the literature explaining the distinction between an SoS and a monolithic system as well as addressing different challenges in the SoS domain including architecture principles, modeling frameworks and methodologies (e.g., [5]- [9]).

Regarding time-triggered schedule generation, there is not enough work on solving scheduling problems for SoS networks. However, several works addressed the scheduling of real-time communication in monolithic distributed embedded systems. In [10], the authors developed two heuristic scheduling algorithms based on GA and List Scheduling (LS) to schedule time-triggered flows in a time-sensitive network combining routing and scheduling constraints. In [11], a hybrid GA was proposed for scheduling time-triggered traffic of Ethernet networks in a dynamic environment. Schweissguth et al. applied an scheduler based on the Integer Linear Programming (ILP) to optimize the scheduling problem in time-triggered Ethernet networks supporting application-specific cycle times and evaluated the performance of their model for different network topologies [12].

Incremental scheduling in monolithic distributed embedded systems is a well-researched problem. The first study in the incremental design of distributed embedded systems was by Pop et al. [13]. They proposed an incremental design process for a broadcast communication channel designed for realtime applications. They map and schedule new applications so that the previous schedules are not disturbed. In [14] they discussed the implications of an incremental design process in the context of a fixed-priority preemptive scheduling policy. Schoeler et al. [15] proposed an incremental scheduling model based on the Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) approach to compute static schedules in a multi-cluster system and compared the results with an optimal scheduler based on Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP).

Several works have introduced different scheduling policies in real-time networks to deal with overloaded systems in a dynamic environment. In [16] authors proposed a novel framework to handle possible overloads while the tasks are dynamically scheduled in a single processor environment. The framework executes a sequence of approximate scheduling algorithms while adjusting the load and refining the quality of the solution. In [17], an approach was developed for process scheduling in computer systems which was used in control applications such as spacecraft. The authors introduced a besteffort service as a rejection policy for overloaded systems by removing tasks with the minimum value density. The proposed scheduler was evaluated in a real-time system simulator for a heavily loaded system. In [18] authors introduced the timesensitive software-defined network architecture and proposed various ILP-based scheduling algorithms to compute and update the schedules of dynamically changing time-triggered flows in the network.

All aforementioned solutions are applied for monolithic distributed systems, which are not compatible with the constraints of an SoS. The closest study to our work is [19], where the incremental scheduling in time-triggered SoS networks is addressed, but it is focused on optimizing each application individually, i.e., not considering the requirements of future applications, which is the main contribution of our work. In this paper, we develop a heuristic approach to compute timetriggered schedules for a sequence of incrementally added SoS applications in a real-time SoS network.

div.head: III. SYSTEM ARCHITECTURE
div.p: The physical elements of an SoS are constituent systems (CSes) and Network Domains (NDs), each can have a complex internal structure which is not visible for other components. Figure 1 depicts an example of the physical model for an SoS with nine components. The CS network comprises endsystems and switches which are shown by ES and SW, respectively. The ND network includes switches to handle the message-based communication between CSes.

An SoS application consists of distinctive services with precedence constraints. Each service possesses jobs and messages which are organized in a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). The internal structure of each service will be realized in a corresponding CS. Figure 2 shows the logical model of an SoS application with five services, each having its own internal structure, and six time-triggered SoS messages. The scheduling model for an SoS application is defined in two scopes: SoS and CS. SoS-level scheduling is done by one of the CSes, namely the one that initiates the new SoS application. CS-level scheduling is done autonomously inside each CS, satisfying the constraints provided by the SoSlevel. First the SoS-level scheduler generates time intervals for the services satisfying their respective dependencies and the overall deadline of the application, as well as selecting a fitting CS for each service. It also conducts the scheduling of the messages between CSes (SoS-messages). In our model, the SoS-level scheduler does not need knowledge about the internals of CSes. Thereafter, the CS-level scheduler inside each CS generates time-triggered schedules of jobs and messages from the assigned service with respect to its determined time slot from the SoS level.

div.head: IV. INCREMENTAL SCHEDULING ALGORITHM
div.p: In the incremental scheduling problem, SoS applications are introduced over time, each one getting corresponding resource allocations that need to be considered in the future SoS applications. It is assumed that each application arrives after finishing the scheduling the prior application. For a new application, an initiator is defined to take care of the SoSlevel scheduling, as well as assigning a corresponding CS for each service. The initiator is determined dynamically based on where an SoS application is requested. The initiator of each application interacts with the local schedulers using the twolevel scheduling algorithm established as a GA.

div.head: A. SoS-Level Scheduling
div.p: For each application, first the SoS-level scheduler is run to generate global solutions for the local CS-level schedulers. The output of the SoS-level of scheduling are multiple solutions, each mapping services to target CSes, their earliest start time and deadlines as well as route selection and setting deadlines for the SoS-message. Figure 3 shows an example of an SoSlevel schedule which will be sent to local schedulers. The example shows the allocation of services (S0 to S4) to CSes as well as their executing time slots, i.e., the earliest start time and the latest finish time of these services. Additionally, there is information about the earliest injection time and the latest arrival time of SoS messages denoted by SoS m .

div.head: B. CS-Level Scheduling
div.p: The CS-level scheduling problem has the following characteristics:

• Service deadline: Each service should be executed in a time period which is determined by the SoS-level scheduler based on the deadline of the associated SoS application. • Real-time jobs: Each job is characterized by its deadline, resource requirements, and the worst case execution time (WCET). • Precedence constraint between the jobs: We define the order of executing jobs regarding to this constraint. • Time-triggered messages: Each message is sent by a job and must be delivered within its deadline. • Communication costs: It is assumed that there is a communication cost to transmit messages from a job on one end-system to a succeeding job on a different end-system. The communication cost between two tasks on the same end-system is assumed to be zero. Figure 4 gives an overview of the proposed two-level interactive scheduling in the time-triggered SoS.

div.head: C. Resource allocation strategy
div.p: In the proposed scheduling model, each CS local scheduler decides how to assign its resources, i.e., the end-systems and switches, for executing jobs and transmitting messages of a service. The first allocation strategy is to select the earliest available time slot for jobs and messages aiming at minimizing the makespan. This allocation approach may cause unbalanced working time assignment for the resources but it works efficiently for an individual application as long as there is no need to share the resources with other applications. However, in real cases different applications emerge over time, while the resources are still occupied by the previous applications and a shortage of resources for the future applications is probable. In order to have a more balanced resource assignment, we have to save enough free time slots beforehand for upcoming applications.

Therefore, we propose a second allocation strategy focusing on creating more balance in the blocking times of resources. We develop an incremental scheduler with maximum blocking time consideration (MBT-aware scheduler). The MBT is computed for each resource as the longest occupied time interval which depends on a given threshold parameter called delta. In calculating the MBT of a resource, when the idle time slot between two consecutive working time slots is shorter than delta, this time slot will be treated like a busy time slot for the scheduler as it is not enough to be assigned to any future jobs and messages. The MBT of a CS is the maximum MBT among resources. The goal of the new incremental scheduler is to minimize the MBT of CSes as well as the makespan of the SoS application. The determination of an efficient value of the parameter delta depends on the specifications of a problem, e.g., the WCET of jobs and the hop time in each CS network.

In figure 5, we show the difference in the scheduling outcomes from two incremental schedulers using the two mentioned allocation strategies. The problem is to assign the resources of a CS to the service with 3 jobs from 3 different SoS applications which are incrementally added to the network with 2 end-systems (es0 and es1) connected through a switch (sw0). In this example, we assume that both the WCET for all jobs and the hop time are equal to 20 ms.

As figure 5 shows, the first incremental scheduler runs all the jobs of the first application on the same end-system (es0) to save time, because there is no communication cost. When the second application appears, it has to run the jobs on the other end-system (es1). The non MBT-aware incremental scheduler generates schedules with the shortest makespan for these two applications, but it is not possible to assign the current resources to the application 2. Contrarily, the second incremental scheduler establishes the MBT-makespan trade-off and accepts the communication cost which results from using all the resources in a more balanced way. As a result, it is capable of scheduling all three applications.

div.head: D. GA Design
div.p: Algorithm 1 shows the structure of the proposed two-level incremental GA scheduler with MBT consideration. The GAbased scheduler is run for each application separately upon the release time of the application. For each SoS application, the initiator creates a set of SoS-level schedules and sends them to the corresponding CS, where the local scheduler must determine a schedule within the given time interval. Afterwards the CS unrolls the service and establishes a DAG with jobs to be scheduled inside the CS. The local schedule comprises the temporal and spatial resource allocation such as assigning jobs to end-systems, the allocation of messages to paths between end-systems, execution time of jobs and injection time of messages. These local schedules will minimize the fitness function based on the MBT of all resources and the lateness of the service with respect to its deadline provided by the initiator.

After completing the scheduling process, each CS returns the fittest schedule and its fitness value to the SoS level. The initiator collects the results and determines a global fitness for each solution (i.e., SoS-level schedule) based on the maximum lateness and fitness value of CSes. The initiator updates the initial population P using mutation and cross-over based on the global fitness. Thereafter, the initiator requests new solutions from the CS, which subsequently lead to new fitness values and new global solutions. This iterative process is stopped once the deadline of the SoS application is satisfied.

div.head: V. EXAMPLE SCENARIOS AND RESULTS
div.p: We examined the performance of the MBT-aware incremental scheduler by generating a set of SoS scenarios based on the Stanford Network Analysis Package (SNAP) library [20]. The generated example scenario includes an SoS network with 4 CSes and 3 NDs, in addition to 10 real-time SoS applications which are released incrementally in a chronological order to be executed over time. We compare the schedules resulting from the two GA-based incremental schedulers with different allocation strategies and fitness functions. Table II presents the main parameters of the GA, which are tuned for both schedulers in order to obtain better results. Table III compares the average makespan of the 10 applications obtained from both schedulers as well as the shortest makespan of each application in case of scheduling individually. Regarding to these results, the MBT-aware incremental scheduler outperforms the incremental scheduler without blocking time consideration. Although the non MBT-aware scheduler found better results (shorter makespan) for the first and second applications, its performance was getting worse by releasing more applications and eventually it was not able to meet the deadline for the 9th and 10th applications (The deadlines for all applications are assumed as 3 ms). On the other hand, the MBT-aware scheduler could cope better with the upcoming applications. One of the demanding parameters in the MBT-aware incremental scheduler is delta, which affects the performance of the allocation process and consequently the makespan of schedules. We examined different values of this parameter and its effect on the performance of our scheduler. As figure 6 shows, by increasing the value of delta from 0 to 20, the schedule results are enhanced significantly, but by increasing this value beyond 25 or 30 has a reverse effect on the performance of the incremental scheduler. As figure 7 shows, the best value for the parameter W 0 is 0.6, which has the highest rank of success. The success ratio is defined as the number of SoS applications found schedulable by the scheduler divided by the total number of applications. VI. CONCLUSION In this paper, we proposed a two-level heuristic algorithm to incrementally schedule real-time SoS applications by adding them to a TTSoS network. To cope with the challenge of reserving resources of the TTSoS for future applications, we developed a new allocation approach, which provides balanced working time assignments for resources and focusing not only on optimizing the present application but also sparing time slots for the upcoming applications. We evaluated the incremental scheduler with the new allocation approach on 10 generated applications. The experimental results show the schedulability and the improvement compared to the conventional one.
